summary:
The Servicemember Quality of Life Improvement and National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2025 (Public Law 118-159, enacted December 23, 2024, originating as H.R. 5009) authorizes appropriations for Department of Defense (DoD) military activities, military construction, and Department of Energy (DOE) national security programs, and prescribes military personnel levels for fiscal year 2025. It is organized into seven divisions covering DoD authorizations, military construction, DOE national security, funding tables, other matters, intelligence, and State Department authorization.

**Funding.** The Act authorizes procurement appropriations totaling $167,849,488,000 (up from a $166,377,384,000 request) and operation and maintenance funds of $294,464,130,000. Research, development, test, and evaluation authorizations include $14,285,551,000 (Army), $26,356,323,000 (Navy), and $48,723,211,000 (Air Force). Notable procurement adjustments include increases for Precision Strike Missiles, Counter-Small UAS intercept systems, Patriot and Stinger modifications, and Abrams upgrades, offset by reductions to programs such as the Joint Light Tactical Vehicle and Long-Range Hypersonic Weapon. Cooperative Threat Reduction receives targeted amounts, including $209,858,000 for biological threat reduction. General transfer authority is capped at $6,000,000,000.

**Compensation and personnel.** Effective April 1, 2025, the Act reforms basic pay tables (e.g., E-1 at $2,319.00/month; O-10 with 20+ years at $18,808.20). It raises the health professions accession bonus from $20,000 to $100,000 and the skill proficiency bonus maximum from $12,000 to $55,000, and expands the Basic Needs Allowance income threshold from 150% to 200% of poverty. It extends parental leave to Coast Guard Reserve members (effective October 1, 2025) and expands postpartum fitness accommodations to pregnancy loss and stillbirth. Recruiting provisions expand Selective Service data sharing (effective 120 days after enactment), guarantee military recruiter campus access under ESEA (effective one year after enactment), and create a two-year pilot delegating reserve medical waiver authority for up to three disqualifying conditions.

**Organization and acquisition.** The Act establishes an Office of Expanded Competition within the Air Force to counter adversarial capital flows, a Counter-UAS Task Force (within 30 days), and requires strategies for countering domestic UAS incursions (report due June 1, 2025). It makes permanent the pilot program for contractor distribution support and extends several acquisition pilots (e.g., streamlined innovative-technology awards to October 1, 2029). It limits low-rate production options on certain cost-reimbursement contracts to one and creates middle-tier acquisition pathways (2–5 years).

**Reports and strategic requirements.** The Act mandates numerous plans and studies, including a biotechnology roadmap (within one year, sunsetting after 10 years), quantum information science and electromagnetic spectrum plans, an Army Centralized Security Monitoring Program plan (due September 1, 2025), tactical fighter force structure reports, and reviews of DoD construction roles. Aircraft floors and extensions are adjusted, including lowering the A-10 minimum from 135 to 96 aircraft and extending RQ-4 authority to September 30, 2029.

**Foreign and space matters.** Provisions require plans to reconstitute U.S. Forces Japan as a joint force headquarters (within 180 days), strengthen extended deterrence to South Korea (March 1, 2025), and enhance trilateral cooperation with Japan and Korea. The Vietnam wartime accounting initiative is expanded and extended to October 1, 2031. Space provisions modify National Security Space Launch policy through 2029, require consolidated monthly notifications of foreign interference with space capabilities, and establish a hybrid satellite communications pilot.

**Military construction and other divisions.** Division B extends and modifies numerous Guard/Reserve facility projects (e.g., relocating a Vermont readiness center to Lyndon), authorizes a Naval Innovation Center at the Naval Postgraduate School, and provides assistance to expedite Guam construction. Division G (State Department authorization) creates rest and recuperation leave (up to 20 days) and overseas operations leave (up to 10 days), an Overseas Crisis Response System, and commercial spyware protection standards. Intelligence provisions expand public-private talent exchanges (details extended to five years) and designate ransomware threats to critical infrastructure as national intelligence priorities.
